title: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
answer: Explaining models to regulators and clients is the practice of translating how a model was built, what data it used, and how it behaves into terms a non-specialist overseer can check. It sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because the people asking are usually accountable for the outcome, not for the code. The audience is typically a supervisor, an internal risk committee, an auditor, or a client's procurement and legal team. The work covers documentation, testing evidence, and a plain account of limits and failure modes.

sections.body: Explaining models to regulators and clients is the practice of translating how a model was built, what data it used, and how it behaves into terms a non-specialist overseer can check. It sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because the people asking are usually accountable for the outcome, not for the code. The audience is typically a supervisor, an internal risk committee, an auditor, or a client's procurement and legal team. The work covers documentation, testing evidence, and a plain account of limits and failure modes.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The material behind an explanation usually lives in a model card or system card, a data lineage record, validation reports, and logs of past decisions. Teams keep these in model registries and documentation repositories so a version can be tied to the evidence that describes it. Monitoring dashboards supply the ongoing behaviour, such as drift, error rates, and override rates.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by fixing the question the explanation must answer, then choose the level of detail the audience can act on. They separate what the model does from why it was chosen, and they show testing against defined cases rather than asserting good behaviour. Feature importance, counterfactual examples, and simple worked cases are common ways to make behaviour concrete. The explanation is reviewed by someone who did not build the model, and the review is recorded.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Accountability rests with the firm and its named owners, not with the model or its vendor. Explanations must be accurate, so overstating what a model can do creates its own liability, and regulators increasingly expect the same account given to clients. Provenance matters: where the data came from, who approved its use, and what consent or contract covers it. The site tracks 153 active AI lawsuits, a reminder that these accounts can later be tested in dispute.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expectation is moving from one-off documents toward continuous evidence that a model still behaves as described. Regulators are asking for explanations that survive staff changes and vendor swaps, which pushes firms toward standard formats and machine-readable records. Clients are beginning to ask the same questions as supervisors, so the two audiences are converging. The open problem is keeping an explanation honest as models are updated, since a clear account of an old version is of little use.
